slides.title: Computing on Bits: Boolean Algebra

In a letter to A. Marquand (1886), Peirce suggests using electrically operated switches called relays for «and» and «or» operations

points: Back then: relays!
Today: transistors!
Good that we're not dealing with electromechanics anymore ;-)

slides.title: Computing on Bits: Logic Gates
points: There is a voltage on the output Q only if there is a voltage on both inputs A and B
Only if both inputs A and B are set to TRUE, the output Q is set to TRUE: that's an AND

aside.alt: Symbols of six logic gates: OR, AND, XOR, NOR, NAND and NOT, each with inputs A and B and output Q
aside.caption: Symbols for logic gates

callout.text: Exclusive Or: «Either A or B, but not both!»

slides.title: XOR Function: Q = (A XOR B)

callout.text: Exclusive Or: «Either A or B, but not both!»

slides.after: We'll need this as well for our computer… ;-)

slides.title: Computing on Bits: NAND
points: Henry Sheffer (1882-1964): functional completeness of NAND
All operations over a binary number space can be represented using combinations of NOT-AND («NAND») gates
Equivalently: all logic operations can be computed with combinations of NAND gates
Proofs: [Wikipedia: NAND logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAND_logic)

aside.alt: Symbol of a NAND gate with inputs A and B and output Q

slides.title: If a NAND receives the same input twice, it computes a NOT
slides.after: With A = B, only the first and the last row occur: Q = NOT A.

slides.title: How to Build a NAND Gate?
points: Two transistors, T1 (input A) and T2 (input B), between the output Q and ground
A pull-up resistor connects Q to the supply voltage (e.g., 5 volts)
So we need two transistors to produce a NAND. We produce billions of transistors per second…
We can compute with lots of NANDs ;-)

aside.alt: Circuit diagram of a NAND gate: two transistor switches T1 and T2 in series under a resistor to +Vcc, with the truth table beside it

slides.title: It's easier to see than you think!
rows: 1: Q is connected to the supply voltage (via the pull-up resistor)
1: Q is connected to the supply voltage
1: Q is connected to the supply voltage
0: the supply voltage is connected to ground, Q carries no voltage
slides.after: That's the NAND function, Q = (A NAND B): that's what we wanted!!

slides.heading: Take-Home
points: Through standard encodings, any symbol can be represented as a binary number
We can (relatively easily and cheaply) create NAND gates
Combinations of NAND gates can express all logic functions, and thus all functions over a binary number space
slides.after: Therefore, we have a universal calculator (or, «computer»). At least in principle; we'll build it next ;-)

slides.title: Let's build a Calculator!

callout.text: How do we do pen-and-paper additions?

paragraphs: You already know how to do this; you just need to transfer some knowledge from school.
As we have seen, in binary, logic and arithmetic are equivalent. So we should be able to do this calculation with a circuit of only NAND gates.
slides.after: And if we can add, we can also multiply, subtract, divide… ([remember](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/01-information/html/#/19))

slides.title: Now YOU build a Calculator!

callout.text: Teams of two: what's the meaning of «sum» and «carry» in binary?

points: You have two inputs, A and B, which are both binary digits
You have two outputs, S(um) and C(arry), which are both binary digits
If a bit A and a bit B go in, S should hold the sum while C should hold the carry
Example: A = 1 and B = 1 should yield S = 0 and C = 1

aside.code:
1b
+  1b
-----
  10b

The «0» is the sum bit S
The «1» is the carry bit C

slides.title: Walkthrough
items: Which value (0/1) does S need to assume if A/B are 0/0, 0/1, 1/0 or 1/1?
With which logical expression can you express S = A ?? B?
With which logical expression can you express C = A ?? B?
Can you draw your calculator using the logic gate symbols?

aside.alt: Symbols of six logic gates: OR, AND, XOR, NOR, NAND and NOT

slides.title: A Half-Adder Adds Two Bits
points: The sum output should be 0 if both inputs are 0. It should also be 0 if an overflow occurs. In other words, it should be 1 if either A or B is 1 (but not both). That's an **exclusive OR**!
The carry output should be 1 if both A and B are 1. That's an **AND**!

aside.alt: Circuit of a half-adder: inputs A and B go to an XOR gate with output S and to an AND gate with output C

slides.title: Let's build a LARGER Adder

callout.text: What's the physical size of this circuit (i.e., in cm)?

points: 1× 8-bit adder = 8× 1-bit adders that are connected properly
2× XOR + 2× AND + 1× OR per full adder: 40 gates in total, about 80 transistors in total
Inputs a0 … a7 and b0 … b7, result s0 … s7, and a carry-out

aside.alt: An 8-bit adder: eight full adder blocks in a row with the carry chained through

slides.title: How large is our 8-bit adder?
slides.lead: About 80 transistors at about 25 nm each:
points: 2000 nm if chained in a straight line (+ wiring)
225 nm × 225 nm if arranged in a 2D grid («rectangle»)
125 nm × 125 nm × 125 nm if arranged in a 3D grid («cube»)

points: Through (smart) combinations of logic gates, we can build adding circuits, and you did this!
Through (smart) combinations of logic gates, we can also build subtractors, multipliers, etc.
These can be produced in mass quantities and at extremely low prices and sizes

groups.heading: Basic Depth
points: Play nandgame.com, and understand it! (I'm serious)
Read up on circuits and [logic gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_gate), and understand [adder circuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adder_%28electronics%29)
Keep internalizing number representations, especially hexadecimal ([lecture 1](https://hyperdecks.github.io/computersystems/01-information/html/#/52))
Get prepared for the exercise session
